Often when friends plan a long trip, this question comes up: 

> Why take a slow night train when a plane is so much faster?

Let me take a stab at answering this more completely.

## First, why you shouldn’t

Night trains are not for everyone, and in fact, there are plenty of travellers who will be happier flying.

Some ways to know if you are **not** a good fit for a sleeper:

* You cannot sleep with motion
* You need to arrive at an exact hour
* You want a large private bathroom
* You like planning each meal ahead of time
* You prefer one long leg over several short ones
* You think of travel time as lost time
* You would rather nobody shared your compartment
* You don’t want to carry your own bag on and off
* You dislike being woken by a border check

Now this isn’t an all or nothing test. Some of these are even easy to work around, and plenty of people who tick two or three boxes still love the night train once they have tried it with the right ticket and a good pair of earplugs.

## The upside

You might think that the main upside of a night train is the saved hotel night. It is real: you sleep and travel at once, and you wake up in the middle of a city instead of at an airport an hour outside it, with your whole first day still ahead of you.

It’s difficult to put fair numbers on this. Flights look cheaper until you add the trip to the airport, the early arrival, the bag fees, and the train into town at the other end. Night trains look slower until you remember that you would have been asleep anyway. For many routes in Europe the door to door time ends up closer than most people expect, and the morning is far calmer.

## The journey

A more reliable pleasure of the night train is not the arrival, but the ride itself.

When I took my first sleeper as a student, an older passenger said something I still remember:

> This will be the slowest trip you take and the one you remember longest.

That feeling is common on night trains. If you choose the right route, you will see things that no plane window shows, and you will end up talking to people you would never meet in a departure lounge or a crowded airport queue.

* You will watch towns go past in the last light of the evening
* You will share tea in the corridor with someone from another country
* You will wake at a small station in the mountains while the train waits

It may test your patience, but if the train is comfortable this will feel like a gift.

Imagine falling asleep to the rhythm of the rails and knowing that you will wake up somewhere completely new in the morning.

Imagine standing in the corridor at midnight while the lights of a city slide past the window and the rest of the carriage sleeps.

Imagine sharing breakfast in the dining car with a stranger who turns out to know the best bakery in the town you are both headed to.

Imagine stepping off onto the platform rested and calm, with your bag over your shoulder and the whole day ahead of you, no taxi needed.

This is the trade. Slow and memorable. 

No rush, no stress (as they say).

## A big “if”

Not all night trains are equal. Just because a route runs overnight, does not mean it is pleasant.

If you’ve read this far and still want to try a sleeper, these are the things worth checking first:

* A real bed: some trains only offer reclining seats, which are fine for a short hop but miserable for a whole night. Look for a couchette or a sleeper compartment, and check how many people share it before you book the ticket.
* Good timing: the best routes leave in the early evening and arrive after breakfast. Trains that arrive at four in the morning leave you on a cold platform with nothing open.
* Clear booking: the operator should show the exact compartment type, the number of berths, and what is included. If the booking page is vague, call or ask at the station. A clear answer before the trip saves an argument in the corridor at midnight.
* Food on board: there is no perfect rule here, but check whether the train has a dining car, a trolley, or nothing at all. On long routes, bring water, fruit and something warm to drink, because the one shop at the last station may already be closed when you pass.
